newsitem.title: CHINA: New HK government gets down to business.
newsitem.headline: New HK government gets down to business.

text.p: Hong Kong's new post-colonial government launched into its first full week of business on Monday, gearing up for a key cabinet meeting and a legislative session that will set the tone for the future.

Tung Chee-hwa, chosen by a Beijing-controlled committee to lead the new Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, is set to convene his advisory cabinet, the Executive Council, on Tuesday, officials said.
High on the agenda for Exco, as it is familiarly known, is a crisis over illegal immigration involving thousands of children from mainland China.
It is also expected to discuss what electoral system should replace the one put in place by the British colonial government and scrapped by Beijing on taking back the territory on July 1.

On Wednesday Tung will go to the Stonecutters Island naval base in Victoria harbour to pay a first visit to the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) garrison, whose almost 5,000 troops are responsible for the defence of the Hong Kong SAR.

Under the agreement with Britain which led to last Tuesday's handover, China has promised Hong Kong's 6.4 million people they may keep their freewheeling capitalist lifestyle for half a century. The SAR's government is to enjoy broad autonomy, with Beijing responsible only for defence and foreign affairs.

Tung's advisory cabinet consists of pro-China politicians and tycoons, plus three top civil servants in charge of key government departments, including popular Chief Secretary Anson Chan and Finance Secretary Sir Donald Tsang.
Exco is to set out the new government's priorities for bills to be presented to the Provisional Legislature, officials said.

The highly controversial, unelected legislature -- which China set up to replace the assembly elected under British auspices in 1995 -- is to hold its first regular post-handover session on Wednesday.
"We have to wait for tomorrow's Exco meeting to see whether the government will table any bills (at the legislature)," an official at the legislature's secretariat said.

Chief Executive Tung and his 15 close advisers are widely expected to tackle the crisis over a tide of illegal immigration from mainland China, overwhelmingly children smuggled into Hong Kong to join parents who are already residents.

Hundreds of families have taken their children to Hong Kong's immigration office in the past few days to register and apply for residency rights, believing the new government will not send them back to the mainland.

Most of the "child illegals" have Hong Kong fathers and, under the territory's post-handover constitution, have the theoretical right to live here. The problem is that many relatives have jumped the gun, sneaking the children in without waiting to obtain formal clearance from the authorities.
It is estimated that 60,000 children from "split families" are waiting to settle in Hong Kong.

Exco's discussions on a proposed new electoral system are important because, until rules can be drawn up and new legislative elections held, Tung will have to field accusations that the unelected interim chamber is unconstitutional.

Tung has promised that the first post-handover election will be held in the second quarter of 1998. He is now pondering which system should be used -- how many geographical seats to establish, and whether to use proportional representation.
Tung and his advisory body also face pressure from the business community to find a way to strike down labour laws passed by the old chamber in the dying days of British rule.

The legislation boosted trade unions' collective bargaining power. Pro-business Liberal Party legislator James Tien said on Monday that, if the post-colonial government did not scrap the laws, his party would do it with a private member's bill.
"(The new law) means business will be run by union leaders -- not by businesses," Tien said.
"We certainly think it's a very bad signal sent to international investors right at this stage just forming the Special Administrative Region," Tien told reporters.
